hints: Time to the top is u/g, so the whole flight lasts nu/g. Use one equation for the whole flight from the top of the tower to the ground.
worded:
1. Time to the highest point is u/g, so the time to the ground is nu/g.

2. Over the whole flight the displacement is H downward. One equation of motion, with the time nu/g, links H, u and n.

3. Quick check on the options: if n = 2 the particle is back at the top of the tower exactly when it “hits the ground”, so H must be 0. (A) fails this; (B), (C) and (D) pass.

4. Second check: for a very tall tower (large n) the short climb hardly matters, and the flight is almost a drop lasting nu/g. Then H ≈ ½g(nu/g)², i.e. 2gH ≈ n²u². (C) matches this; (B) gives twice as much and (D) grows only like n. So (C).

**No-pen route: limiting cases.** Steps 3 and 4 settle it without algebra: H = 0 at n = 2 rules out (A), and “almost a drop” for large n (2gH ≈ n²u²) rules out (B) and (D).
conventional:
![](asset:P000113-sol-1)

Take up as positive, origin at the top of the tower; the ground is at $y = - H$. Time to the ground $t = nu/g$:

$$- H = u\left( \frac{nu}{g} \right) - \frac{1}{2}g\left( \frac{nu}{g} \right)^{2} = \frac{nu^{2}}{g} - \frac{n^{2}u^{2}}{2g}.$$

$$2gH = n^{2}u^{2} - 2nu^{2} = nu^{2}(n - 2).$$
mistakes: Take the displacement to the ground as −H (below the launch point), not +H.
Use one equation for the whole flight; there is no need to split it at the top.
